## One function, one answer

`stabl()` is the one-stop-shop entry point to **stablr**.  You give it a
table of features and an outcome; it runs STABL with statistically safe
defaults and returns an object that tells you, in plain language, which
features were selected and how reliable the selection is estimated to be.

That is the whole contract:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit <- stabl(my_data, y = "response")
fit
```

Everything else in the package is available when you need more control —
see "The expert layer" below.

## A worked example

We simulate a small proteomic-style dataset: 60 samples, 8 features, of
which two truly drive the outcome.

```{r data}
set.seed(1L)
df <- data.frame(
  m1 = rnorm(60), m2 = rnorm(60), m3 = rnorm(60), m4 = rnorm(60),
  m5 = rnorm(60), n1 = rnorm(60), n2 = rnorm(60), n3 = rnorm(60)
)
df$response <- 0.9 * df$m1 + 0.9 * df$m2 + rnorm(60, sd = 0.4)
```

Fit STABL.  Here we lower the number of bootstraps so the vignette knits
quickly; the default (`n_bootstraps = 1000`) is what you should use in
practice.

```{r fit, message = FALSE}
library(stablr)
fit <- stabl(df, y = "response", n_bootstraps = 200L, random_state = 1L)
```

Printing the fit gives the plain-language answer:

```{r print}
fit
```

The selected features, as a character vector:

```{r names}
feature_names(fit)
```

`summary()` adds the stability threshold and the FDP+ estimate;
`plot()` draws the stability paths and the FDP+ curve:

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

```{r plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit)
```

## What `stabl()` does for you

| Decision | Default chosen | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Artificial features | model-X knockoffs (`knockoff_equi`) | the pairing validated for FDP+ calibration; the raw `random_permutation` default of the expert interface is anti-conservative for multivariate learners |
| Calibration | FDP+ on (no fixed `hard_threshold`) | the threshold is chosen to control the estimated false discovery proportion rather than fixed by hand |
| Knockoff failure | `knockoff_fallback = "stop"` | a silent fallback would silently change what the FDP+ estimates mean |
| Lambda grid | automatic | a sensible grid is derived from the data |

Any expert argument — `artificial_proportion`, `sample_fraction`,
`sample_groups`, a custom adapter — is one `...` away:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit <- stabl(df, y = "response", base_learner = "elastic_net",
             artificial_proportion = 0.5)
```

## The expert layer

`stabl()` is a thin, opinionated wrapper around `stabl_fit()`, the expert
interface with full control over all arguments (lambda grids, bootstrap
design, thresholds, learner adapters, grouping).  Every `stabl()` result
is also a valid `stabl_fit` object, so the whole expert toolkit applies
unchanged:

```{r expert}
# accessors (identical on stabl and stabl_fit objects)
head(get_stabl_scores(fit))
get_fdrs(fit)

# the multiomic workflows, metrics, and plotting helpers all accept
# stabl_fit objects — including the one you just built with stabl()
class(fit)
```

Read `?stabl_fit` for the full expert interface, and the other vignettes
for multi-omic workflows, nested cross-validation, and environment
stability.

## If you used the package before 0.3.0

Nothing is removed.  A handful of ambiguous names were renamed
(`get_feature_names_out()` is now `get_feature_names()`,
`stacked_multi_omic()` is now `stabl_multiomic_stacked()`,
`jaccard_matrix()` is now `jaccard_similarity_matrix()`, and so on — see
`NEWS.md` for the full table).  The old names still work: each warns once
and delegates to the new name.
